report.tagline: An Indian AI company that builds language and voice models for Indian languages and sells them to businesses and government.
report.simpleSummary: Sarvam builds AI that understands and speaks Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other Indian languages. Banks and insurers use its voice bots to call crores of customers in their own language. Developers pay to use its models through an API. It also has a free chat app called Indus, like a home-grown ChatGPT.

overview.whatItDoes: Sarvam trains its own large AI models (Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B) and speech models that work well in Indian languages. It sells these to businesses as voice agents, document reading tools and an API. It also runs Indus, a consumer chat app. Its pitch is 'sovereign AI', meaning AI built and run in India that Indian firms and government can control.
howItWorks: Sarvam trains models on Indian-language text and speech using its own GPUs in India.
Developers call the models through an API and pay per use.
Enterprises use ready products: voice agents for sales and support calls, Sarvam Vision for reading documents, and work agents for internal tasks.
Sarvam's own engineers work inside big clients to set up these tools (forward-deployed work).
Consumers use the Indus app to chat by typing or speaking in their language.
Some models are open source, so anyone can download and run them.
overview.valueProposition: For Indian businesses and government: AI that speaks the customer's language, keeps data inside India and costs less than foreign AI. For users: an assistant that understands how Indians actually talk, including mixed Hindi-English.

painPoints.pain: Most AI models work best in English and struggle with Indian languages and accents.
painPoints.howSolved: Models trained on Indian languages, including speech models Saaras (listening) and Bulbul (speaking).

painPoints.pain: Calling crores of customers with humans is very expensive.

painPoints.pain: Banks and government can't send sensitive data abroad.
painPoints.howSolved: Models hosted in India, and open models that clients can run themselves.

painPoints.pain: Paper and handwritten records can't be searched.
painPoints.howSolved: Sarvam Vision reads Indian-language documents; 3.5 crore+ pages digitised.

painPoints.pain: Foreign AI costs a lot in dollars.
painPoints.howSolved: Pricing set to undercut international providers.

businessModel.summary: Sarvam makes money mostly from businesses and government. It charges enterprises for voice agents and custom AI projects, charges developers per API use, and earns from hosting models for others. The Indus app is free.

revenueStreams.detail: Banks, insurers and fintechs pay for voice agents, sales tools and work agents, often with setup help.
Ministries and states pay for voice outreach and document digitisation.
Developers pay per call, per minute of audio or per amount of text.
Firms pay to train models on their own data.

businessModel.pricing: Pay-as-you-go API pricing in rupees on the developer platform, said to be lower than global rivals. Enterprise and government pricing is not public. Indus is free.
costDrivers: GPUs and electricity to train and run models (moving from 2,000 to 10,000 GPUs)
Top AI researchers and engineers, often paid global salaries
businessModel.unitEconomics: Think of one voice call. A human agent call in India may cost ₹10 to ₹20 once salary and office costs are added. If Sarvam's bot handles a 2-minute call for a few rupees, the client saves money and Sarvam keeps the gap between its price and its GPU cost. The catch is training: building a new big model costs crores of rupees up front, and that only pays off if many clients use it. These numbers are estimates; Sarvam does not publish prices per client or revenue.

growth.moat: Deep focus on Indian languages and voice, data and compute inside India, and close ties with government and big Indian firms. Global AI firms can match model quality, but trust on data, local language quality and on-site teams take years to build.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Google has distribution; Sarvam offers India-run, customisable models for regulated firms.

pmLessons: Pick a niche giants underserve. Sarvam won with Indian voice and local data, not by trying to beat ChatGPT at everything.
In B2B AI, the first sale often needs engineers on site. Turning that into a self-serve product is how it scales.
A consumer app can be a showcase, not the main business.
Trust (data in India, open models) can be a product feature for regulated customers.
Compute cost decides AI pricing. Using the smallest model that works protects margin.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Sarvam focus on Indus (consumers) or enterprises?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare revenue, cost of free users and competition with ChatGPT. Argue enterprise first, keep Indus as a feedback and brand tool.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure if a voice agent for an insurer is working?
interviewQuestions.hint: Task completion, renewal rate versus humans, cost per call, complaints and handover rate.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you price Sarvam's speech API?
interviewQuestions.hint: Per minute, in rupees, tiered by volume. Anchor below global rivals and above GPU cost. Offer free credits to start.

interviewQuestions.question: Global AI firms now support Hindi. How does Sarvam stay relevant?
interviewQuestions.hint: Go deeper: dialects, code-mixed speech, phone audio, data residency, on-site support and government trust.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a product for farmers using Sarvam's tech.
interviewQuestions.hint: Voice-first by phone call, local language, mandi prices and weather, works on feature phones. Measure repeat calls and actions taken.
